claim: Cancer treatment by radiation or chemotherapy triggers the release of excess serotonin from the mucosal enterochromaffin cells in the upper gastrointestinal tract.
source: Cancer treatment by radiation or chemotherapy triggers the release of excess serotonin from the mucosal enterochromaffin cells in the upper gastrointestinal tract (Schwörer et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwörer et al., 1991

claim: Serotonin binds to 5-HT3Rs on the vagal afferent nerve in the gut and on the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the brainstem leading to severe nausea and vomiting in patients receiving cancer treatments.
source: Serotonin binds to serotonin (3) receptors (5-HT3Rs), a pentameric ligand-gated ion channel (pLGIC), on the vagal afferent nerve in the gut and on the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the brainstem leading to severe nausea and vomiting in patients receiving cancer treatments.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about serotonin receptor function

claim: Uncontrolled debilitating side effects of cancer treatment result in secondary complications such as dehydration and anorexia that require additional hospitalization and increase overall healthcare costs.
source: Furthermore, uncontrolled debilitating side effects result in secondary complications such as dehydration and anorexia that require additional hospitalization and increase overall healthcare costs.
evidence: General medical knowledge about complications of uncontrolled nausea and vomiting

claim: Setrons are competitive antagonists of 5-HT3R and are effective in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV), radiation therapy-induced nausea and vomiting (RINV), and postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV).
source: Setrons, competitive antagonists of 5-HT3R, are effective in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV), radiation therapy- induced nausea and vomiting (RINV), and postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) (Spiller, 2011; Hsu, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Spiller, 2011 and Hsu, 2010

claim: The first generation of FDA approved setrons are effective for treating acute but not delayed phase nausea due to their short plasma half-lives.
source: The first generation of FDA approved setrons are effective for treating acute but not delayed phase nausea due to their short plasma half-lives.
evidence: Established pharmacological knowledge about first-generation setrons

claim: Palonosetron is the only FDA approved second generation setron and is shown to have a longer half-life, improved bioavailability, and efficacy.
source: The isoquinoline derivative palonosetron, the only FDA approved second generation setron, is shown to have a longer half-life, improved bioavailability, and efficacy.

claim: Palonosetron is implicated in causing receptor internalization, which further improves antiemetic properties.
source: In addition, palonosetron is implicated in causing receptor internalization, which further improves antiemetic properties.

claim: The FDA approved treatment of diarrhea-predominant IBS with alosetron led to severe ischemic colitis in many patients.
source: For example, the FDA approved treatment of diarrhea-predominant IBS with alosetron led to severe ischemic colitis in many patients (Friedel et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Friedel et al., 2001

claim: 5-HT3Rs are the only ion channels among the large family of serotonin receptors, the rest being G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: 5-HT3Rs are the only ion channels (Maricq et al., 1991) among the large family of serotonin receptors, the rest being G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maricq et al., 1991

claim: 5-HT3Rs are expressed as homopentamers of subunit A or heteropentamers of subunit A, in combination with B, C, D, or E subunits.
source: 5-HT3Rs are expressed as homopentamers of subunit A or heteropentamers of subunit A, in combination with B, C, D, or E subunits (Niesler et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Niesler et al., 2007

claim: Compositional and stoichiometric differences lead to differential responses to serotonin, gating kinetics, permeability, and pharmacology.
source: Compositional and stoichiometric differences lead to differential responses to serotonin, gating kinetics, permeability, and pharmacology (Davies et al., 1999; Kelley et al., 2003; Thompson and Lummis, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davies et al., 1999; Kelley et al., 2003; Thompson and Lummis, 2013

claim: Granisetron, palonosetron, ondansetron, and alosetron have slightly different affinities for various receptor subtypes.
source: Of note, granisetron, palonosetron, ondansetron, and alosetron have slightly different affinities for various receptor subtypes (Gregory and Ettinger, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gregory and Ettinger, 1998

claim: Ondansetron binds to several GPCRs, such as 5-HT1BR, 5-HT1CR, α1-adrenergic receptors and μ-opioid receptors, in addition to binding to 5-HT3Rs.
source: Ondansetron, in addition to binding to 5-HT3Rs, also binds to several GPCRs, such as 5-HT1BR, 5-HT1CR, α1-adrenergic receptors and μ-opioid receptors (Kovac, 2016).

claim: Granisetron binds to all subtypes of 5-HT3R, but has little or no affinity for 5-HT1R, 5-HT2R and 5-HT4R receptors.
source: Granisetron binds to all subtypes of 5-HT3R, but has little or no affinity for 5-HT1R, 5-HT2R and 5-HT4R receptors.

claim: Palonosetron is highly selective for 5-HT3AR and dolasetron for 5-HT3ABR.
source: Palonosetron is highly selective for 5-HT3AR and dolasetron for 5-HT3ABR (Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2012

claim: Cryo-EM structures of full-length 5-HT3AR in complex with palonosetron, ondansetron, and alosetron were solved at the resolution range of 2.9 Å to 3.3 Å.
source: In the present study, we have solved cryo-EM structures of the full-length 5-HT3AR in complex with palonosetron, ondansetron, and alosetron at the resolution range of 2.9 Å to 3.3 Å.
evidence: Experimental data from cryo-EM structure determination

claim: The final three-dimensional reconstruction achieved a nominal resolution of 3.3 Å for 5-HT3AR-Palono (with 91,163 particles), 3.0 Å for 5-HT3AR-Ondan (67,333 particles), and 2.9 Å for 5-HT3AR-Alo (42,065 particles).
source: Iterative classifications and C5 symmetry-imposed refinement produced a final three-dimensional reconstruction at a nominal resolution of 3.3 Å for 5-HT3AR-Palono (with 91,163 particles), 3.0 Å for 5-HT3AR-Ondan (67,333 particles), and 2.9 Å for 5-HT3AR-Alo (42,065 particles) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: Experimental data from cryo-EM structure determination

claim: The local resolution of the map was in the range of 2.5–3.5 Å for each of the setron-bound 5-HT3AR reconstructions.
source: The local resolution of the map was estimated using ResMap and in the range of 2.5–3.5 Å for each of these reconstructions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Experimental data from cryo-EM structure determination

claim: Each of the setron-bound 5-HT3AR complexes has an architecture similar to previously solved 5-HT3A receptors.
source: Overall, each of the setron-bound 5-HT3AR complexes has an architecture similar to previously solved 5-HT3A receptors (Polovinkin et al., 2018; Hassaine et al., 2014; Basak et al., 2018a; Basak et al., 2018b).
evidence: Comparison with previously published structures cited

claim: Three sets of peripheral protrusions corresponding to N-linked glycans are bound to the Asn82, Asn148, and Asn164 in each subunit.
source: Three sets of peripheral protrusions corresponding to N-linked glycans are bound to the Asn82, Asn148, and Asn164 in each subunit (Figure 1a, right).
evidence: Observed in cryo-EM density maps and structural models

claim: A strong, unambiguous density is seen at each of the intersubunit interfaces, corresponding to individual setrons.
source: A strong, unambiguous density is seen at each of the intersubunit interfaces, corresponding to individual setrons (Figure 1b).

claim: No additional densities for setrons were found beyond the orthosteric binding site under the experimental conditions used.
source: Besides this site, no additional densities for setrons were found under these conditions, although there have been predictions that palonosetron may act as both an orthosteric and allosteric ligand (Del Cadia et al., 2013).

claim: Setrons bind within the canonical neurotransmitter-binding pocket and are lined by residues from Loops A, B, and C on the principal (+) subunit and Loops D, E, and F from the complementary (-) subunit.
source: Setrons bind within the canonical neurotransmitter-binding pocket and are lined by residues from Loops A, B, and C on the principal (+) subunit and Loops D, E, and F from the complementary (-) subunit (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Residues within 4 Å of setron include Asn101 in Loop A, Trp156 in Loop B, Phe199, and Tyr207 in Loop C, Trp63 and Arg65 in Loop D, and Tyr126 in Loop E.
source: Residues within 4 Å of setron include Asn101 in Loop A, Trp156 in Loop B, Phe199, and Tyr207 in Loop C, Trp63 and Arg65 in Loop D, and Tyr126 in Loop E.

claim: These binding site residues are strictly conserved, and perturbations at each of these positions impact efficacy of setrons and serotonin.
source: These residues are strictly conserved, and perturbations at each of these positions impact efficacy of setrons and serotonin (Yan et al., 1999; Duffy et al., 2012; Thompson et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yan et al., 1999; Duffy et al., 2012; Thompson et al., 2005

claim: In each setron-5-HT3AR complex, the essential pharmacophore of the setron is placed in a similar orientation: the basic amine is at the deep-end of the pocket in the principal subunit; the defining aromatic moiety interacts with residues in the complementary subunit; and the carbonyl-based linker, between the two groups, is essentially coplanar with the aromatic ring.
source: In each setron-5-HT3AR complex, the essential pharmacophore of the setron is placed in a similar orientation: the basic amine is at the deep-end of the pocket in the principal subunit; the defining aromatic moiety interacts with residues in the complementary subunit; and the carbonyl-based linker, between the two groups, is essentially coplanar with the aromatic ring.

claim: In the 5-HT3AR-Alo structure, the carbonyl oxygen of Trp156 forms a hydrogen bond with the amine group in the diazole ring of alosetron.
source: In particular, the carbonyl oxygen of Trp156 is close to the amine group of setron, and in the 5-HT3AR-Alo, it forms a hydrogen bond with the amine group in the diazole ring.

claim: The relative orientation of the tertiary nitrogen and Trp156 is conducive for a cation-pi interaction.
source: The relative orientation of the tertiary nitrogen and Trp156 is conducive for a cation-pi interaction, as seen in the AChBP-5-HT3 chimera structure (Kesters et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference from structural geometry and comparison with cited structure

claim: A similar cation-pi interaction is predicted for the primary amine group of serotonin with Trp156.
source: A similar interaction is also predicted for the primary amine group of serotonin (Beene et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beene et al., 2002

claim: The aromatic end of setrons is oriented toward the complementary subunit and lies parallel to the membrane.
source: It is oriented toward the complementary subunit, and lies parallel to the membrane.

claim: The aromatic moiety of setrons is stabilized by a number of hydrophobic interactions with Ile44, Trp63, Tyr64, Ile201, and Tyr126.
source: In this orientation, the aromatic moiety is stabilized by a number of hydrophobic interactions with Ile44, Trp63, Tyr64, Ile201, and Tyr126 (shown by gray color in surface representation Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed in cryo-EM structures and confirmed by MD simulations

claim: The setron molecule is within 4–5 Å and potentially makes π-π interactions (edge-to-face or face-to-face) with Trp63, Tyr126, Trp156, and Tyr207.
source: The setron molecule is within 4–5 Å and potentially makes π-π interactions (edge-to-face or face-to-face) with Trp63, Tyr126, Trp156, and Tyr207.
evidence: Inference from structural distances and confirmed by MD simulations

claim: The planar aromatic rings of setrons lie beneath Arg65 and are in close proximity to the positively charged nitrogen in the guanidinium group of Arg65, revealing a potential cation-pi interaction.
source: In addition, the planar aromatic rings lie beneath Arg65, and are in close proximity to the positively charged nitrogen in the guanidinium group of Arg65, revealing a potential cation-pi interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: The setron position causes reorientation of Arg65 (β2 strand or Loop D) and Trp168 (β8-β9; Loop F).
source: As previously noted in 5-HT3AR-Grani, the setron position causes reorientation of Arg65 (β2 strand or Loop D) and Trp168 (β8-β9; Loop F) (Basak et al., 2019).
evidence: Observed in cryo-EM structures and comparison with previous structure

claim: Large orientational differences for Trp168 were predicted when the binding site was occupied by agonist or antagonist.
source: Earlier reports also predicted large orientational differences for Trp168 when the binding site was occupied by agonist or antagonist (Thompson et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thompson et al., 2006

claim: In the setron-bound structures, Arg65 is in a network of interactions involving Asp42 (β1), Try126 (β6), Trp168 (β8-β9; Loop F), Arg169 (β8-β9; Loop F), and Asp177 (β8-β9; Loop F).
source: In this position, Arg65 is in a network of interactions involving Asp42 (β1), Try126 (β6), Trp168 (β8-β9; Loop F), Arg169 (β8-β9; Loop F), and Asp177 (β8-β9; Loop F) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).

claim: Both the Arg65 and Glu102 interaction networks are present in serotonin-bound 5-HT3AR, but absent in 5-HT3AR-Apo, indicating the ligand-induced formation of the interaction network.
source: Interestingly, both of these networks are also present in serotonin-bound 5-HT3AR, but absent in 5-HT3AR-Apo, indicating the ligand-induced formation of the interaction network (Basak et al., 2018a; Basak et al., 2018b).

claim: 100 ns MD simulations were carried out for 5-HT3AR-Grani, 5-HT3AR-Palono, 5-HT3AR-Ondan and 5-HT3AR-Alo structures embedded in a POPC membrane and encased in water with 150 mM NaCl.
source: To understand the dynamics of ligand-receptor interactions, 100 ns MD simulations were carried out for 5-HT3AR-Grani, 5-HT3AR-Palono, 5-HT3AR-Ondan and 5-HT3AR-Alo, structures embedded in a 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl phosphatidyl choline (POPC) membrane and encased in water with 150 mM NaCl.

claim: The serotonin molecule exhibited considerable fluctuations (RMSD up to 5.4 Å with an average value of 1.9 Å, across five subunits) within the binding pocket during MD simulations.
source: Among the ligands studied, the serotonin molecule exhibited considerable fluctuations (RMSD up to 5.4 Å with an average value of 1.9 Å, across five subunits) within the binding pocket.

claim: Most setron molecules maintained a low RMSD (RMSD average values of 1.1 Å, 1.0 Å, and 1.1 Å for granisetron, ondansetron, and alosetron, respectively) during MD simulations.
source: In contrast, most setron molecules maintained a low RMSD (RMSD average values of 1.1 Å, 1.0 Å, and 1.1 Å for granisetron, ondansetron, and alosetron, respectively), with palonosetron demonstrating the largest RMSD (1.9 Å) among all the simulated setrons (Figure 3a).

claim: Palonosetron demonstrated the largest RMSD (1.9 Å) among all the simulated setrons.
source: In contrast, most setron molecules maintained a low RMSD (RMSD average values of 1.1 Å, 1.0 Å, and 1.1 Å for granisetron, ondansetron, and alosetron, respectively), with palonosetron demonstrating the largest RMSD (1.9 Å) among all the simulated setrons (Figure 3a).

claim: During the simulation, the palonosetron's bicyclic ring displayed fluctuation and positional reorientation with distinct interactions with binding-site residues, in particular with Asn101 in the 'down' position and Trp156 in the 'up' position.
source: During the simulation, the palonosetron's bicyclic ring displayed fluctuation and positional reorientation. In these orientations, palonosetron had distinct interactions with binding-site residues, in particular with Asn101 in the 'down' position and Trp156 in the 'up' position (Figure 3b and c).

claim: A recently reported structure of 5-HT3AR in complex with palonosetron shows an overall similar conformation of the protein as seen in this study.
source: A recently reported structure of 5-HT3AR in complex with palonosetron (published during revision of this manuscript) shows an overall similar conformation of the protein as seen here (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Zarkadas et al., 2020).

claim: The bicyclic ring orientation of palonosetron reported in the Zarkadas et al. structure is similar to that captured in the MD simulations of this study.
source: Interestingly, the bicyclic ring orientation reported in this structure is similar to that captured in our MD simulations.
evidence: Comparison between MD simulation results and independently published structure

claim: In the 5-HT3AR-Serotonin simulations, the indole ring of serotonin makes pi-pi stacking interactions with key aromatic residues Trp63, Tyr126, Trp156, and Tyr207, with only interactions with Trp156 and Tyr126 occurring with probability larger than 50%.
source: In the 5-HT3AR-Serotonin simulations, the indole ring of serotonin makes pi-pi stacking interactions (edge-to-face or face-to-face) with key aromatic residues Trp63, Tyr126, and Trp156, and Tyr207. Among these only interactions with Trp156 and Tyr126 occur with probability larger than 50%.

claim: Mutations to each of the aromatic positions Trp63, Tyr126, Trp156, and Tyr207 affect serotonin-binding and are reflected in increase in EC50 for activation.
source: Mutations to each of these aromatic position affects serotonin-binding and is reflected in increase in EC50 for activation (Beene et al., 2002; Spier and Lummis, 2000; Beene et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beene et al., 2002; Spier and Lummis, 2000; Beene et al., 2004

claim: The indole nitrogen of serotonin forms water-mediated interactions with Asp42 and Arg169 with a 25% probability during MD simulations.
source: The indole nitrogen of serotonin forms water-mediated interactions with Asp42 and Arg169, albeit with a 25% probability whereas the ligand's hydroxyl group forms a hydrogen-bond with the amine nitrogen of Trp156 with a 50% probability.

claim: The hydroxyl group of serotonin forms a hydrogen-bond with the amine nitrogen of Trp156 with a 50% probability during MD simulations.
source: The indole nitrogen of serotonin forms water-mediated interactions with Asp42 and Arg169, albeit with a 25% probability whereas the ligand's hydroxyl group forms a hydrogen-bond with the amine nitrogen of Trp156 with a 50% probability.

claim: The primary amine nitrogen in serotonin makes multiple water-mediated interactions with the side chains of Glu209 and Thr154, and occasionally with Asn101 (less than 25% of the simulation time).
source: The primary amine nitrogen in serotonin makes multiple water-mediated interactions with the side chains of Glu209 and Thr154, and occasionally with Asn101 (less than 25% of the simulation time).

claim: Serotonin forms relatively stable apolar interactions (>50% probability) with Ile44, Phe199, and Ile201 during MD simulations.
source: In addition, serotonin forms relatively stable apolar interactions (>50% probability) with Ile44, Phe199, and Ile201.

claim: All setrons form a number of very stable (probability >75%), mostly apolar, interactions with the following residues: Asp42, Val43, Ile44, Trp63, Tyr64, Arg65, Tyr126, and Trp156.
source: The structural fingerprint analysis shows that all setrons form a number of very stable (probability >75%), mostly apolar, interactions with the following residues: Asp42, Val43, Ile44, Trp63, Tyr64, Arg65, Tyr126, and Trp156.

claim: In 5-HT3AR-Grani, the bicyclic nitrogen makes water-mediated hydrogen bonds with the sidechains of Thr154, Ser155, and Glu209.
source: In 5-HT3AR-Grani, the bicyclic nitrogen makes water-mediated hydrogen bonds with the sidechains of Thr154, Ser155, and Glu209.

claim: Reduced affinity for granisetron is noted upon mutations at positions Trp63, Trp156, and Tyr207, and notably W63A, W156A, and Y207A do not bind granisetron.
source: Reduced affinity for granisetron is noted upon mutations at these positions (Yan et al., 1999) and notably W63A, W156A, and Y207A do not bind granisetron.
evidence: Supported by citation to Yan et al., 1999

claim: In 5-HT3AR-Palono, the tertiary amine on the ligand's bicyclic ring makes water-mediated and direct polar contacts with the backbone oxygen of Trp156 or the sidechain of Asn101 depending on the orientation of bicyclic ring.
source: In 5-HT3AR-Palono, the tertiary amine on the ligand's bicyclic ring makes water-mediated and direct polar contacts with the backbone oxygen of Trp156 or the sidechain of Asn101 depending on the orientation of bicyclic ring.

claim: The carbonyl group of the isoquinoline moiety of palonosetron interacts with the amine nitrogen of Trp156 and carbonyl oxygen of Tyr64 through a water molecule.
source: The carbonyl group of the isoquinoline moiety interacts with the amine nitrogen of Trp156 and carbonyl oxygen of Tyr64 through a water molecule.

claim: Mutations of Trp156 or Tyr64 cause large or small increases of palonosetron-induced inhibition, respectively.
source: Mutations of Trp156 or Tyr64 cause large or small increases of palonosetron-induced inhibition, respectively (Price et al., 2016; Del Cadia et al., 2013; Beene et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Price et al., 2016; Del Cadia et al., 2013; Beene et al., 2002

claim: While N101Q preserves palonosetron-induced inhibition similar to wild-type receptor, a mutation to N101A increases the potency of palonosetron.
source: Interestingly, while N101Q preserves palonosetron-induced inhibition similar to wild-type receptor, a mutation to N101A (no H-bond with side chain) increases the potency of palonosetron (Price et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Price et al., 2016

claim: Palonosetron forms an apolar interaction with Arg169 with higher probability compared to the other ligands, potentially due to palonosetron's pose forming weak interactions with loop C in favor of loop F.
source: Palonosetron forms an apolar interaction with Arg169 with higher probability compared to the other ligands, potentially due to palonosetron's pose forming weak interactions with loop C in favor of loop F.
evidence: Data from MD simulations and inference about mechanism

claim: In 5-HT3AR-Ondan, the ondansetron molecule forms highly probable edge-to-face stacking interactions with Tyr126 and Tyr207.
source: In 5-HT3AR-Ondan, the ondansetron molecule forms highly probable edge-to-face stacking interactions with Tyr126 and Tyr207.

claim: The secondary nitrogen on the diazole ring of ondansetron forms a hydrogen-bond interaction with Glu209 through a water molecule.
source: The secondary nitrogen on the diazole ring forms a hydrogen-bond interaction with Glu209 through a water molecule.

claim: In 5-HT3AR-Alo, one of the secondary amine nitrogen on the diazole ring forms a water-mediated hydrogen-bond interaction with the carbonyl oxygen of Trp156.
source: In 5-HT3AR-Alo, one of the secondary amine nitrogen on the diazole ring forms a water-mediated hydrogen-bond interaction with the carbonyl oxygen of Trp156.

claim: Water-mediated interactions with Glu209 are absent in the alosetron fingerprint when compared to the ondansetron, granisetron, and serotonin fingerprints.
source: Interestingly, water-mediated interactions with Glu209 are absent in the alosetron fingerprint when compared to the ondansetron, granisetron, and serotonin fingerprints.

claim: Many of the ligand-receptor interactions identified as important by the MD simulations are not directly evident from the Cryo-EM structures particularly since many of these interactions are mediated through water molecules.
source: It is to be noted that many of the ligand-receptor interactions identified as important by the MD simulations are not directly evident from the Cryo-EM structures particularly since many of these interactions are mediated through water molecules (not modeled in the structural coordinates).
evidence: Comparison between cryo-EM structures and MD simulation results

claim: MD simulation captures several transient interactions arising from side-chain flexibility and drug mobility within the pocket.
source: In addition, MD simulation captures several transient interactions arising from side-chain flexibility and drug mobility within the pocket.

claim: 5-HT3AR-Grani revealed a counter-clockwise twist of beta strands in the ECD leading to a small inward movement of Loop C closing-in on granisetron.
source: We previously showed that instead of being in a 5-HT3AR-Apo like conformation, 5-HT3AR-Grani revealed a counter-clockwise twist of beta strands in the ECD leading to a small inward movement of Loop C (connecting β9-β10 strands) closing-in on granisetron (Basak et al., 2019).

claim: The Loop C conformation has been correlated to the agonistic nature of the ligand in the binding site.
source: The Loop C conformation has been correlated to the agonistic nature of the ligand in the binding site.
evidence: Established knowledge from pLGIC structural studies

claim: The AChBP-ligand complexes have shown that agonist binding induces a 'closure' of Loop C, capping the ligand-binding site.
source: The AChBP-ligand complexes have shown that agonist binding induces a 'closure' of Loop C, capping the ligand-binding site (Hansen et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hansen et al., 2005

claim: Studies have shown that unliganded pLGIC gating kinetics remain unaffected by Loop C truncation, raising ambiguity over the role of Loop C closure in channel opening.
source: However, studies have shown that unliganded pLGIC gating kinetics remain unaffected by Loop C truncation (Purohit and Auerbach, 2013), raising ambiguity over the role of Loop C closure in channel opening.
evidence: Supported by citation to Purohit and Auerbach, 2013

claim: Antagonist-bound AChBP structures show that Loop C further extended outward.
source: Antagonist-bound AChBP structures show that Loop C further extended outward (Hansen et al., 2005), while partial agonists seem to induce partial Loop C closure but not to the level achieved by agonists (Hibbs et al., 2009), suggesting a correlation between the degree of Loop C closure and the level of agonism.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hansen et al., 2005 and Hibbs et al., 2009

claim: In the crystal structure of AChBP in complex with antagonist dihydro-β-erythroidine, Loop C appears to move inward.
source: However, in the crystal structure of AChBP in complex with antagonist dihydro-β-erythroidine, Loop C appears to move inward (Shahsavar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shahsavar et al., 2012

claim: In comparison to the 5-HT3AR-Apo structure, Loop C adopts varying degrees of an inward conformation in setron-bound structures, and in the 5-HT3AR-Alo structure the orientation is similar to 5-HT3AR-serotonin.
source: In comparison to the 5-HT3AR-Apo structure, Loop C adopts varying degrees of an inward conformation, and in the 5-HT3AR-Alo structure the orientation is similar to 5-HT3AR-serotonin (Basak et al., 2019; Figure 4a).

claim: The twisting inward movement of Loop C is shared by adjoining β7, β9 and β10 strands forming the outer-sheets of the β-sandwich core, with notable deviations from the corresponding regions in the 5-HT3AR-Apo structure.
source: The twisting inward movement does not pertain to Loop C alone, but it is also shared by adjoining β7, β9 and β10 strands forming the outer-sheets of the β-sandwich core, with notable deviations from the corresponding regions in the 5-HT3AR-Apo structure (Figure 4b).

claim: Only minimal changes are observed in the β-strands of the inner sheets (β1, β2, β6) in setron-bound structures compared to 5-HT3AR-Apo.
source: In contrast, only minimal changes are observed in the β-strands of the inner sheets (β1, β2, β6) (Figure 4b and c).

claim: When reporter-groups were introduced in Loop C of 5-HT3AR, similar fluorescence changes were recorded from binding either serotonin or setrons.
source: When reporter-groups were introduced in Loop C of 5-HT3AR, similar fluorescence changes were recorded from binding either serotonin or setrons (Munro et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Munro et al., 2019

claim: In GlyR, both glycine (agonist) and strychnine (a competitive antagonist) produced identical fluorescence responses from labels in certain regions of Loop C.
source: In GlyR, both glycine (agonist) and strychnine (a competitive antagonist) produced identical fluorescence responses from labels in certain regions of Loop C (Pless and Lynch, 2009), and a similar trend was also observed in ρ1GABAR (Chang and Weiss, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pless and Lynch, 2009 and Chang and Weiss, 2002

claim: The inner β-sheet regions (particularly Loop E, contributing to the binding pocket from the complementary subunit) undergo distinct movements depending on the nature of the bound ligand in GlyR, 5-HT3AR, and GABAAR.
source: Interestingly, the inner β-sheet regions (particularly Loop E, contributing to the binding pocket from the complementary subunit) undergo distinct movements depending on the nature of the bound ligand in GlyR, 5-HT3AR, and GABAAR (Munro et al., 2019; Pless and Lynch, 2009; Chang and Weiss, 2002; Muroi et al., 2006) suggesting that this region maybe a better reporter for ligand discrimination.
evidence: Supported by citations to Munro et al., 2019; Pless and Lynch, 2009; Chang and Weiss, 2002; Muroi et al., 2006

claim: Loop C is stable in its initial cryo-EM conformation in the case of 5-HT3AR-Alo and 5-HT3AR-Serotonin simulations where it predominantly adopts a 'closed' conformation.
source: Comparing these two parameters across the different systems suggest that Loop C is stable in its initial cryo-EM conformation in the case of 5-HT3AR-Alo and 5-HT3AR-Serotonin simulations where it predominantly adopts a 'closed' conformation.

claim: In other setron complexes, Loop C is observed to switch to an alternate 'open' conformation where it extends away from the binding-site surface.
source: In other setron complexes, Loop C is observed to switch to an alternate 'open' conformation where it extends away from the binding-site surface.

claim: Loop C exhibited a much larger flexibility in 5-HT3AR-Apo as evidenced by large RMSD values and a wide-range of dihedral angles.
source: In comparison to all the ligand-bound structures, Loop C exhibited a much larger flexibility in 5-HT3AR-Apo as evidenced by large RMSD values and a wide-range of dihedral angles.

claim: The presence of a ligand in the binding-site forces the loop C to remain 'closed'.
source: These multiple Loop C 'opening' and 'closing' events in the 5-HT3AR-Apo structure contrasts ligand-bound states of the channel and suggest that the presence of a ligand in the binding-site forces the loop C to remain 'closed'.

claim: Enhanced flexibility of Loop C in the unliganded state of 5-HT3AR has been reported in a previous 20 μs simulation study.
source: Such enhanced flexibility in the unliganded state of 5-HT3AR has also been reported in a previous 20 μs simulation study (Guros et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guros et al., 2020

claim: Alosetron, ondansetron, and serotonin have a relatively lower number of water molecules within their binding sites compared to other setrons.
source: These data show that alosetron, ondansetron, and serotonin have a relatively lower number of water molecules within their binding sites (Figure 5).

claim: The 5-HT3AR-Alo and 5-HT3AR-Serotonin MD simulations maintained an interaction between Arg65 and Asp202 more often than in any other setron-bound structure.
source: We find that the 5-HT3AR-Alo and 5-HT3AR-Serotonin MD simulations maintained an interaction between Arg65 and Asp202 more often than in any other setron-bound structure, and that most setron-bound simulations did not appreciably form this stabilizing interaction (Figure 6a and b).

claim: When Arg65 is interacting with Asp202, Loop C is in a stable 'closed' conformation, which in turn reduces the accessibility of the binding pocket to water, and contributes to the higher stability of the ligand binding pose.
source: Thus, our mechanistic hypothesis is such that when Arg65 is interacting with Asp202, Loop C is in a stable 'closed' conformation, which in turn reduces the accessibility of the binding pocket to water, and incidentally contributes to the higher stability of the ligand binding pose.

claim: Mutations at the Arg65 position in human 5-HT3AR abolish granisetron binding but tropisetron binding is only reduced.
source: In agreement, mutations at the Arg65 position in human 5-HT3AR abolish granisetron binding but tropisetron binding is only reduced (Ruepp et al., 2017).

claim: The R65A mutation has a significant effect on inhibition by each setron, albeit to varying extents.

claim: In each of the 5-HT3AR-setrons structures, the pore-lining M2 helices are positioned away from the central axis, and are in a more-expanded conformation than in the 5-HT3AR-Apo structure.
source: Interestingly, in each of the 5-HT3AR-setrons structures, the pore-lining M2 helices are positioned away from the central axis, and are in a more-expanded conformation than in the 5-HT3AR-Apo structure (Figure 7a).

source: At positions Val264 (13′), Leu260 (9′), Ser253 (2′), and Glu250 (−1′), the pore radii in 5-HT3AR-setron structures are larger than in the 5-HT3AR-Apo structure.

claim: In all setron-bound structures, the pore is constricted to below the hydrated Na+ radii.
source: However, in all these structures, the pore is constricted to below the hydrated Na+ radii (Marcus, 1988; Figure 7b).

claim: No major changes to the overall pore profile of the channel were observed during 100 ns MD simulations.
source: As expected, no major changes to the overall pore profile of the channel were observed during simulations, which were carried out in the absence of positional restraints.

claim: In each case, the pore remained constricted at the Leu260 (9′) position to under 2.3 Å during MD simulations.
source: Most notably, in each case, the pore remained constricted at the Leu260 (9′) to under 2.3 Å (below the hydrated Na+ radius).

claim: The Leu260 (9′) position is the major barrier in the TMD to ion permeation in the 5-HT3AR-Apo and 5-HT3AR-Serotonin structures.
source: As also reported in earlier simulation studies, the Leu260 (9′) position is the major barrier in the TMD to ion permeation in the 5-HT3AR-Apo and 5-HT3AR-Serotonin structures (Basak et al., 2018b).
evidence: Data from MD simulations and comparison with previous studies

claim: The post-M3 loop occludes the lateral portals at the interface of the TMD and ICD in setron-bound structures, and the extent of occlusion is similar to that seen in the 5-HT3AR-Apo structure.
source: While there are small conformational changes in the ICD, the post-M3 loop occludes the lateral portals at the interface of the TMD and ICD which are predicted to be the ion exit paths. The extent of occlusion is similar to that seen in the 5-HT3AR-Apo structure (Basak et al., 2018a) suggesting that the ICD exits are closed in these conformations.

claim: In muscle-type nAChR, the ICD portals appear to be open even in the Apo conformation, highlighting the mechanistic differences among pLGIC members.

claim: Although there are different extents of conformational changes in the 5-HT3AR-setron structures that lie between those of 5-HT3AR-Apo and 5-HT3AR-Serotonin, each of these structures appears to be non-conducting to ions.
source: Overall, these analyses suggest that although there are different extents of conformational changes in the 5-HT3AR-setron structures that lie between those of 5-HT3AR-Apo and 5-HT3AR-Serotonin, each of these structures appears to be non-conducting to ions.
evidence: Inference from structural and MD simulation data

source: A sequence alignment of mouse and human 5-HT3R subunits (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) shows that two key residues that interact with serotonin and setrons, Trp156 (on the principal side) and Arg65 (on the complementary side), are present exclusively in subunit A.

claim: The setron-binding site may be limited to A-A interfaces both in the 5-HT3AR homomeric and heteromeric assemblies.
source: This suggests that the setron- binding site may be limited to A-A interfaces both in the 5-HT3AR homomeric and heteromeric assemblies.
